h1: Palisade hops for apricot and grassy notes in pale ales
title: Palisade Hops for Apricot in Pale Ales | Craft Beer School
desc: Palisade hops explained: a Yakima Valley hop with apricot and grassy notes, how to balance them in a pale ale and a 20 litre recipe with dry hop timing.
teaser: Palisade smells of apricot and cut grass. Which one wins depends on how long the hops sit in the beer.
standfirst: Palisade is an American hop with apricot, floral and grassy notes. It is easy to like in a pale ale and easy to overdo. Here is how to push the fruit and keep the grass in the background.
sections:
Palisade is an American aroma hop from the Yakima Valley in Washington State. Brewers use it in pale ales, amber ales and lagers where they want fruit without a heavy tropical punch. Alpha acid sits at a moderate level. We use roughly 7% in the recipe below, but your lot analysis decides the weights.

The aroma is usually described as apricot, stone fruit and floral notes, with a grassy, herbal edge. That grassy part is what divides brewers. Some like it as freshness. Others call it harsh.

Apricot and stone fruit notes come from hop oil compounds that are easily lost in a long boil. The fruit lives in the whirlpool and the dry hop, not at 60 minutes. A late addition at a lower temperature gives more fruit and less green character. A whirlpool at 75 to 80 °C extracts oils without driving them off, which is why the recipe below includes one.

For a fuller picture of orange and floral notes in a similar beer, see Amarillo. If you want something less green and more floral, Loral is worth a comparison.
A 20 litre pale ale with Palisade

Here is a recipe at about OG 1.050 and 35 IBU, giving around 5% ABV:

  • Pale ale malt 4.2 kg (91%).
  • Wheat malt 0.25 kg (5%).
  • Light crystal malt 0.17 kg (4%).
  • Palisade 35 g at 60 minutes for about 30 IBU.
  • Palisade 30 g at 5 minutes.
  • Palisade 30 g in a 20 minute whirlpool at 80 °C.
  • Palisade 60 g dry hop for three days.

Mash at 65 to 66 °C. Ferment with a clean American ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. The wheat malt helps head retention and adds softness.

Aim for a moderate sulphate level in the water, with some chloride for roundness. Sulphate sharpens bitterness and would emphasise the green side of the hop. If your tap water is hard, cut it with RO or boiled and cooled soft water. Taste the first batch before you change anything else.
The floor detail: contact time decides the grass

Dry hop contact is the dial. For three days at 18 °C, the apricot comes through. Leave the same hops in the fermenter for ten days and the beer drifts towards cut grass and hay. If your beer tastes of lawn clippings, shorten the contact before you cut the dose.

The same is true of heat. At 28 to 30 °C, extraction speeds up and grassy compounds arrive sooner. In an Indian summer, a one day dry hop in a warm room can pull as much green character as three days in a cool one. Keep the dry hop cold. If you can, remove the hops by racking or cold crashing after the contact time you chose.

Apricot fades fast. A pack opened in a warm room, or hops stored without freezing, lose the fruit first and leave the green behind. Buy sealed packs, check the harvest year and freeze them. Keep packaged beer cold.

A pale ale that tastes of apricot in week one can taste flat and grassy by week six if it sits in a warm shop. In India, the cold chain is the weak link, so tell friends to keep their bottles in the fridge from day one.

Beyond pale ale, try it in an amber ale, where caramel malt and apricot work together. Try a small late dose in a golden ale or a lager with fruit character. It is less successful in strong dark beers, where it disappears.

On the table, a pale ale with stone fruit notes suits lightly spiced dishes such as tandoori fish or chicken tikka. Our guide on hops for beers that pair with Indian food explains how bitterness and spice interact.

Once you taste both the apricot and the grass in your own beer, you start asking why. The answer is hop chemistry: which compounds extract when, which fade and which oxidise. Advanced Brewing Science covers that in six weeks, with practical sessions on dry hop timing and oxygen control.
faqs: Apricot and stone fruit with floral and grassy notes. The grass shows more with long contact or warm dry hopping.
How long should I dry hop with Palisade?
Three days at a cool temperature is a good start. Longer contact tends to add grassy and hay-like flavours.
It can bitter at moderate alpha acid, but most brewers keep it for late additions where the fruit lives.
Amarillo or Loral give a similar pale ale character with more orange or more floral notes. Adjust weights to the new alpha acid.
